islands.name: Forest
islands.subtitle: Friendly starters, runners and crest collectors.

species.name: Leafy
species.rationale: Leafy is the familiar Velociraptor starter and speedster who anchors the collection.
species.note: Approved selected look is integrated through ranch and dedicated reveal assets. Final motion, voice, habitat and native acceptance remain separate.

habitat.evidence: Leafy is the game’s stylized Velociraptor. Velociraptor fossils are documented from Mongolia and China; the Fighting Dinosaurs specimen was buried in sand. These records do not establish a preference for dense forest.
habitat.caveat: Forest remains Leafy’s approved game placement. Its suitability is a design inference, not a confirmed paleontological habitat match.
habitat.recommendation: Keep Leafy in the locked Forest roster as a game design choice; label the species Velociraptor.

sources.title: Natural History Museum — Velociraptor species and fossil evidence

species.name: Aquilops
species.rationale: Small beak and shield give a second friendly starter silhouette.
species.note: Approved selected look is integrated through ranch and dedicated reveal assets. Final motion, voice, habitat and native acceptance remain separate.

habitat.evidence: Aquilops americanus comes from Montana's Himes Member, Cloverly Formation; regional fluvial floodplains support a plausible woodland-edge setting, without demonstrating forest preference.
habitat.caveat: The known skull's sandy claystone and broader formation reconstruction do not establish its preferred vegetation or microhabitat.
habitat.recommendation: Retain provisionally near open woodland and streams; avoid claiming a confirmed forest specialist.

sources.title: Farke et al. 2014 — Original description and exact Aquilops geological setting
2025 original research — Cloverly ecohydrology and paleoenvironment

species.name: Pachycephalosaurus
species.rationale: A rounded dome makes the head instantly different.
species.note: Approved selected look is integrated through ranch and dedicated reveal assets. Final motion, voice, habitat and native acceptance remain separate.

habitat.evidence: Pachycephalosaurus fossils occur in the Hell Creek Formation, whose warm, moist landscape included forested floodplains, lakes and rivers.
habitat.caveat: Regional habitat evidence does not demonstrate dense-forest specialization or establish its complete habitat range.
habitat.recommendation: Keep in Forest with clearings, dry paths and river margins.

sources.title: Smithsonian — Pachycephalosaurus skull from the Hell Creek Formation
Smithsonian Q?rius — Hell Creek and Lance environments

species.name: Gallimimus
species.rationale: Long legs and small head add height and lightness.
species.note: Approved selected look is integrated through ranch and dedicated reveal assets. Final motion, voice, habitat and native acceptance remain separate.

habitat.evidence: Gallimimus bullatus comes from Mongolia's Nemegt Formation, where isotope evidence supports a seasonal, monsoon-influenced conifer woodland ecosystem.
habitat.caveat: The woodland reconstruction is ecosystem-level; it does not show Gallimimus preferred closed canopy over open areas.
habitat.recommendation: Keep in Forest, emphasizing broad clearings and river corridors.

sources.title: Osmolska et al. 1972 — Original Gallimimus description and Nemegt provenance
Owocki et al. 2020 — Nemegt ecosystem and climate from tooth isotopes

species.name: Stegouros
species.rationale: A squat armored body contrasts with the upright runners.
species.note: Approved selected look is integrated through ranch and dedicated reveal assets. Final motion, voice, habitat and native acceptance remain separate.

habitat.evidence: Stegouros elengassen comes from Chile's Dorotea Formation; its locality lies in a river-and-floodplain succession, making a wet woodland margin plausible.
habitat.caveat: Depositional setting does not establish forest preference; modern subantarctic geography does not establish an ancient snow habitat.
habitat.recommendation: Keep provisionally beside Forest streams and wet clearings; do not describe it as a proven woodland specialist.

sources.title: Soto-Acuna et al. 2021 — Original Stegouros description
2023 original research — Rio de Las Chinas localities and Dorotea depositional environments

species.name: Kentrosaurus
species.rationale: Shoulder and tail spikes supply a clear late-collection silhouette.
species.note: Approved selected look is integrated through ranch and dedicated reveal assets. Final motion, voice, habitat and native acceptance remain separate.

habitat.evidence: Kentrosaurus aethiopicus comes from Tanzania's Tendaguru Formation, whose vegetated hinterland supported conifers and understory under warm, strongly seasonal conditions.
habitat.caveat: Coastal fossil burial does not make it aquatic; seasonal woodland is a better reconstruction than permanently lush tropical jungle.
habitat.recommendation: Keep in Forest with drier clearings, conifers and seasonal vegetation.

sources.title: Museum fur Naturkunde Berlin — Tendaguru collection and Kentrosaurus aethiopicus
Schrank 2010 — Tendaguru pollen, vegetation and paleoclimate

species.name: Parasaurolophus
species.rationale: The long backward crest is a recognisable collection prize.
species.note: Approved selected look is integrated through ranch and dedicated reveal assets. Final motion, voice, habitat and native acceptance remain separate.

habitat.evidence: Parasaurolophus walkeri occurs in Alberta's Dinosaur Park Formation, where plant evidence supports warm-temperate conifer forests and terrestrial browsing.
habitat.caveat: This assessment anchors the genus-level roster name to P. walkeri; other species occur in different formations.
habitat.recommendation: Keep in Forest; identify the intended species as Parasaurolophus walkeri in reference notes.

sources.title: Philip J. Currie Dinosaur Museum — Parasaurolophus walkeri and land-based feeding
Mallon et al. 2013 — Dinosaur Park herbivores, vegetation and feeding-height evidence

species.name: Shunosaurus
species.rationale: A low long neck and tail club finish Forest with a different body plan.
species.note: Approved selected look is integrated through ranch and dedicated reveal assets. Final motion, voice, habitat and native acceptance remain separate.

habitat.evidence: Shunosaurus lii occurs in China's Lower Shaximiao Formation; regional river-and-lake basin deposits make woodland margins plausible, but local forest cover remains insufficiently established here.
habitat.caveat: Formation-wide environments varied; broad basin evidence cannot establish the precise vegetation or preferred habitat at every Shunosaurus locality.
habitat.recommendation: Keep provisionally in open woodland near water; avoid claiming a verified dense-forest habitat.

sources.title: 2022 original research — Shunosaurus material from the Lower Shaximiao Formation
Ma et al. 2023 — Shaximiao sedimentary environments and changing lake/alluvial plains

islands.habitatBrief: Woodland, broad clearings and streams. Aquilops, Stegouros and Shunosaurus have limited habitat-specific evidence.

islands.name: Giants
islands.subtitle: The giant-scale sanctuary and its headline residents.

species.name: Shantungosaurus
species.rationale: Wide muzzle and chunky body make the big herbivore readable.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Existing runtime species; this selected concept look is not proof of matching production animation.

habitat.evidence: A roughly 15-metre terrestrial herbivore; research reconstructs vegetated hills and valleys with plentiful rainfall. Both scale and broad valley habitat suit Giants.
habitat.caveat: The habitat reconstruction is interpretive; its fossils do not establish an exact modern biome or temperature tolerance.
habitat.recommendation: Keep; give it lush vegetation, freshwater and generous open ground.

sources.title: Natural History Museum: Shantungosaurus
Ji et al. (2011): Systematics, Behavior and Living Environment of Shantungosaurus giganteus

species.name: Dreadnoughtus
species.rationale: The towering vertical giant provides the island’s scale fantasy.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Existing runtime species; this selected concept look is not proof of matching production animation.

habitat.evidence: A giant titanosaur from the Cerro Fortaleza Formation; its river-floodplain deposits and regional fossil wood support a forested floodplain setting.
habitat.caveat: Body-mass estimates differ. Burial in a flood deposit does not make it an aquatic dinosaur.
habitat.recommendation: Keep; provide broad land corridors, abundant browsing vegetation and a river valley.

sources.title: Lacovara et al. (2014): A Gigantic, Exceptionally Complete Titanosaurian Sauropod Dinosaur
Schroeter et al. (2022): Dreadnoughtus geological and taphonomic setting

species.name: Giganotosaurus
species.rationale: The large land predator is a clear headline prize.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Selected still approved in the Oct 19 visual baseline. Existing Giga bank is separate; motion identity/finish matching and final native acceptance remain.

habitat.evidence: A very large Candeleros Formation predator; that formation records rivers, alluvial plains and drier open environments, compatible with an open valley mosaic.
habitat.caveat: Regional formation evidence does not prove its precise preferred habitat; uniformly dense, wet forest would be an overstatement.
habitat.recommendation: Keep; retain open terrain, drier patches and river access rather than continuous dense woodland.

sources.title: University of Jaén museum: Giganotosaurus carolinii skull and Candeleros provenance
Candeleros Formation dromaeosaurid-track study: geological and palaeoenvironmental setting

species.name: Therizinosaurus
species.rationale: Long arms and sculpted claws add an unusual upright shape.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Existing runtime species; this selected concept look is not proof of matching production animation.

habitat.evidence: A large Nemegt herbivore associated with a wetter, fertile floodplain ecosystem. Its size and vegetation-rich surroundings support the Giants placement.
habitat.caveat: Its incomplete skeleton limits detailed reconstruction; today's Gobi Desert is not evidence that its ancient habitat was desert.
habitat.recommendation: Keep; include wooded floodplain edges and abundant browsing vegetation.

sources.title: Western Australian Museum: Therizinosaurus
Currie (2016): Dinosaurs of the Nemegt Formation

species.name: Spinosaurus
species.rationale: The sail and long snout separate it from Giga.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Existing runtime species; this selected concept look is not proof of matching production animation.

habitat.evidence: An enormous fish-associated predator with strong ties to waterways and wet margins. Size fits Giants; a token drinking pond would underserve its ecological identity.
habitat.caveat: Active underwater pursuit versus shoreline wading remains debated. Do not present it as a proven deep-diving swimmer.
habitat.recommendation: Keep only with a substantial fish-bearing river, shallow margins and accessible banks.

sources.title: Natural History Museum: Spinosaurus and Baryonyx may have hunted fish underwater
University of Chicago (2024): Spinosaurus shoreline versus underwater hunting debate

species.name: Diplodocus
species.rationale: Long horizontal neck and tail contrast with Dread’s height.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Existing runtime species; this selected concept look is not proof of matching production animation.

habitat.evidence: A giant Morrison Formation sauropod. National Park Service reconstructions place Diplodocus in river-country with open fern vegetation and conifers.
habitat.caveat: The Morrison varied across a large area and through time; it was not one uniform lush forest.
habitat.recommendation: Keep; provide open fern-rich ground, scattered conifers and river access.

sources.title: National Park Service: Morrison Formation Geography
National Park Service: Morrison Formation

species.name: Deinocheirus
species.rationale: Proposed Giants replacement: a huge shaggy body and broad beak give a different silhouette from the long-necks and predators.
species.note: Long arms and broad body need clearance; overlaps Sucho’s large upright role.

habitat.evidence: The Nemegt Formation's giant ornithomimosaur; fish remains and anatomy support an omnivore associated with moist environments. Size fits, but wet habitat matters.
habitat.caveat: Fish in its stomach does not establish that it swam or lived exclusively in water.
habitat.recommendation: Keep with wet floodplain ground, fish-bearing shallows and terrestrial vegetation; Swamp remains another sound option.

sources.title: Lee et al. (2014): Resolving the long-standing enigmas of Deinocheirus mirificus

species.name: Amargasaurus
species.rationale: Proposed Giants replacement: paired neck spines distinguish this smaller long-neck from Dreadnoughtus and Diplodocus.
species.note: Adds another sauropod alongside Giants and Nigersaurus; spine continuity needs work.

habitat.evidence: A roughly 9–10-metre sauropod from La Amarga river-country. Floodplain ecology suits the island, although it was relatively small among sauropods.
habitat.caveat: The concern is the strength of the Giants size theme, not an established ecological mismatch or evidence of snow adaptation.
habitat.recommendation: Ecologically keepable; decide whether Giants includes medium-large animals or only spectacular giants.

sources.title: Western Australian Museum: Amargasaurus cazaui
Salgado et al. (2007): The sauropod diversity of the La Amarga Formation

islands.habitatBrief: A size theme in a varied river valley. Spinosaurus and Deinocheirus need substantial water; Amargasaurus is comparatively small.

islands.name: Swamp
islands.subtitle: Wetlands, shallow water and connected vegetated banks.

species.name: Suchomimus
species.rationale: Keeps the current resident and a tall predator silhouette.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Runtime species exists; selected brighter moss-green concept still needs matching production work.

habitat.evidence: Elrhaz river-floodplain resident; fish feeding and a riverbank/wading interpretation support a freshwater wetland with firm banks.
habitat.caveat: Wading is an interpretation; a deep-diving specialist is unsupported.
habitat.recommendation: Keep beside shallow water and dry banks.

sources.title: University of Chicago: Nigersaurus and its river-floodplain ecosystem
University of Chicago: New analysis continues debate about how Spinosaurus hunted

species.name: Carbonemys
species.rationale: A calm low turtle is a distinct collectible beside the dinosaurs.
species.note: Rigid shell and foot planting need a proof; scope it to the connected banks.

habitat.evidence: A giant freshwater side-necked turtle from tropical Cerrejon; its water association is substantially stronger than a generic swamp aesthetic.
habitat.caveat: A terrestrial-only tortoise portrayal would conflict with its freshwater identity.
habitat.recommendation: Keep with accessible freshwater; flag aquatic behavior work.

sources.title: Florida Museum: Cofrin’s Side-necked Turtle
University of Florida: New extinct giant turtle

species.name: Edaphosaurus
species.rationale: Tall sail plus low body gives Swamp a different shape from Sucho.
species.note: Use ordinary grounded routes; sail and limb continuity still need animation work.

habitat.evidence: Edaphosaurids occur in Early Permian lowland deposits; Edaphosaurus was a plant-processing herbivore. This supports vegetated lowlands, not permanent immersion.
habitat.caveat: Depositional setting does not establish swamp specialization or swimming. It is a synapsid, not a dinosaur.
habitat.recommendation: Keep only on substantial dry, vegetated banks; avoid calling it aquatic.

sources.title: Reisz and Fröbisch 2014: Evolution of herbivory in terrestrial vertebrates

species.name: Nigersaurus
species.rationale: The broad muzzle and low long neck add a gentle herbivore.
species.note: Grounded bank routes; neck and muzzle identity need to survive the motion pass.

habitat.evidence: Known from a lush river floodplain with conifer forests and vegetation, alongside Suchomimus and Sarcosuchus.
habitat.caveat: A terrestrial browser in this landscape; river deposits do not make it a swimmer.
habitat.recommendation: Keep on broad fern-covered banks and floodplain clearings.

sources.title: University of Chicago: More info on Nigersaurus

species.name: Diplocaulus
species.rationale: A wide boomerang head adds a strange, immediately recognisable shape.
species.note: Low splayed contact and wetland access need a separate proof.

habitat.evidence: Aquatic amphibian remains dominate drought-concentrated watercourse deposits; weak limbs support a strongly water-associated lifestyle.
habitat.caveat: Habitat fits, but dry-land-only roaming would be a substantial behavioral fiction.
habitat.recommendation: Keep only with freshwater access and an aquatic presentation plan.

sources.title: Dalquest and Mamay 1963: Permian amphibian concentration in Texas
New Mexico Geological Society: The Permian system at Abo Pass

species.name: Dilophosaurus
species.rationale: Proposed Swamp replacement: twin lengthwise crests bring a clear head shape, distinct from Suchomimus and Snow’s Cryolophosaurus.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Committed ranch and reveal banks exist. Match them against the selected portrait and qualify motion, variants and phones before acceptance.

habitat.evidence: A terrestrial Kayenta predator; the modern redescription allows feeding in local river systems, while emphasizing large terrestrial prey.
habitat.caveat: River association does not establish swamp specialization or an amphibious lifestyle.
habitat.recommendation: Use dry river margins; Forest or Fernlands is equally defensible.

sources.title: Marsh and Rowe 2020: Comprehensive evaluation of Dilophosaurus
University of Texas: Dilophosaurus wetherilli

species.name: Sarcosuchus
species.rationale: Adds a recognisable crocodilian body.
species.note: Long torso/tail turns and bank/water staging expand production scope.

habitat.evidence: Sarcosuchus imperator inhabited African rivers across lush floodplains; a freshwater wetland is a direct ecological match.
habitat.caveat: Needs substantial water; a dry decorative swamp would not represent its river-predator identity.
habitat.recommendation: Keep with river pools and haul-out banks.

sources.title: University of Chicago: Sarcosuchus imperator
University of Chicago: Discovery of Sarcosuchus

species.name: Titanoboa
species.rationale: The most unusual body plan in the Swamp set.
species.note: Continuous coils, crossings and believable whole-body motion carry the highest new risk.

habitat.evidence: Cerrejon fossils come from wet tropical rainforest river systems; the original study inferred an anaconda-like ecology.
habitat.caveat: Aquatic habits are inferred, not directly observed; warm wetland fit is clearer than exact behavior.
habitat.recommendation: Keep in warm freshwater wetlands with water and banks.

sources.title: Head and colleagues 2009: Giant boid snake from the Palaeocene neotropics

islands.habitatBrief: Warm freshwater wetlands with broad dry banks. Aquatic residents need meaningful water access; this is not ground-only habitat.

islands.name: Snow
islands.subtitle: Arctic residents, cool woodland and woolly open-ground grazers.

species.name: Yutyrannus
species.rationale: Keeps the current resident and Snow’s big friendly theropod.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Runtime species exists; this selected periwinkle Snow redesign is still a concept look.

habitat.evidence: The original description documents extensive filamentous feathers. Regional isotope research estimates a cool-temperate Yixian climate, giving a stronger rationale for cold seasonal woodland than for tropical or bare-ice conditions.
habitat.caveat: Direct feather evidence and regional cool-climate evidence do not establish deep-snow tolerance, polar residency or permanent ice adaptation.
habitat.recommendation: Keep in Snow's wooded, seasonal winter habitat with clear ground and shelter.

sources.title: Xu et al. 2012 — Original feathered Yutyrannus description
Amiot et al. 2011 — Early Cretaceous East Asian climate

species.name: Pachyrhinosaurus
species.rationale: Use Pachyrhinosaurus perotorum, the northern Alaskan species, for Snow’s broad-bossed herbivore.
species.note: Existing concept is unchanged and needs a P. perotorum reference check before production acceptance. Preserve its nasal boss; a shaggy coat is not directly established.

habitat.evidence: P. perotorum is explicitly known from northern Alaska. Regional nesting evidence supports year-round dinosaur residency through freezing winters and seasonal snow.
habitat.caveat: Other Pachyrhinosaurus species occurred farther south. The Arctic fossil environment was vegetated and warmer than today's polar icefields. A shaggy coat is not directly demonstrated for this animal.
habitat.recommendation: Keep; use P. perotorum as the art and fact reference and provide woody browse and seasonally snowy ground.

sources.title: University of Alaska Fairbanks — Pachyrhinosaurus perotorum
University of Alaska Fairbanks — Arctic dinosaur nesting and winters

species.name: Woolly Mammoth
species.rationale: Wool, short tusks and a curled trunk make Snow feel special.
species.note: Strong cold-climate fit; a production stretch. Prove trunk and tusk continuity early; accessible forage remains necessary.

habitat.evidence: Cold adaptation and mammoth-steppe association make this one of Snow's clearest anchors.
habitat.caveat: Cold adaptation does not remove the need for abundant accessible plants; continuous deep snow or barren ice is an unsuitable visual shorthand.
habitat.recommendation: Keep in open, windswept forage patches with shallow or broken snow.

sources.title: Natural History Museum — Woolly mammoths and mammoth-steppe habitat
Natural History Museum — Mammoth evolution and cold treeless environments

species.name: Sinosauropteryx
species.rationale: Adds a small, bright collector and more scale variety.
species.note: Long tail and feather cues need phone-size readability checks.

habitat.evidence: Regional isotope evidence supports cool conditions. Countershading analysis independently supports open surroundings, which suits Snow's clearings better than a dense-forest-only island.
habitat.caveat: Neither result proves regular deep-snow use or specialized polar physiology. Its winter placement remains a design inference.
habitat.recommendation: Keep provisionally in sheltered, cool clearings with seasonal, patchy snow.

sources.title: Amiot et al. 2011 — Early Cretaceous East Asian climate
Smithwick et al. 2017 — Sinosauropteryx colour and habitat inference

species.name: Nanuqsaurus
species.rationale: A sturdy tyrannosaur head, short forelimbs and long balancing tail create an Arctic predator alongside Yutyrannus.
species.note: Selected still approved. Feathering is an artistic inference; no direct Nanuqsaurus plumage fossil is known. Its adult size remains under reassessment. No production bank or qualification is claimed.

habitat.evidence: The original description documents an Arctic tyrannosaur. Later regional nesting research supports dinosaurs remaining through freezing, snowy winters.
habitat.caveat: Original material is fragmentary; feathers are an inference, not directly preserved evidence. Its adult size is under reassessment, so do not sell it as an established tiny or dwarf tyrannosaur. The ancient Arctic was vegetated, not a modern ice sheet.
habitat.recommendation: Add as Snow's Arctic tyrannosaur, with winter woodland and open ground. Label any insulating plumage as an artistic reconstruction.

sources.title: Fiorillo and Tykoski 2014 — Original Nanuqsaurus description
University of Alaska Fairbanks — Arctic dinosaur nesting and winters
Perry 2023 — University of Alaska thesis reassessing Nanuqsaurus size and anatomy

species.name: Edmontosaurus
species.rationale: A broad duck bill and deep herbivore body make a readable polar grazer without adding another horned or plated silhouette.
species.note: Selected still approved; refers to Prince Creek Edmontosaurus sp.; species identity is unresolved. No production bank or qualification is claimed.

habitat.evidence: A 2020 cranial reassessment assigns the Arctic hadrosaur material to Edmontosaurus. The locality provides direct high-latitude provenance rather than a visual guess about cold tolerance.
habitat.caveat: The cited study explicitly leaves species unresolved as Edmontosaurus sp.; do not label this population E. regalis or present Ugrunaaluk as an uncontroversial separate species. Arctic did not mean barren ice.
habitat.recommendation: Add a Prince Creek Edmontosaurus, with accessible low vegetation and river-edge habitat. Keep its fact label at genus level.

sources.title: Takasaki et al. 2020 — Arctic Alaskan hadrosaur reassigned to Edmontosaurus sp.
University of Alaska Fairbanks — Arctic dinosaur nesting and winters

species.name: Leaellynasaura
species.rationale: A small biped with a long balancing tail and gentle herbivore head adds scale contrast to Snow’s large residents.
species.note: Selected still approved. Its polar-forest context is better established than its complete anatomy or behaviour; some referred remains are uncertain. No production bank or qualification is claimed.

habitat.evidence: Australian Museum and Museums Victoria describe a cool polar forest with pronounced light seasonality. Regional evidence allows winter ice and seasonally frozen ground, while other fauna suggests generally milder conditions.
habitat.caveat: Polar provenance does not demonstrate a permanent snowfield. Material is limited and some referred bones are uncertain; its exact appearance and behaviour should not be overstated.
habitat.recommendation: Add as Snow's small polar-forest herbivore, using a wooded stream-edge area with seasonal snow and accessible ferns.

sources.title: Australian Museum — Leaellynasaura habitat and evidence limits
Museums Victoria — Leaellynasaura in its cool polar forest

species.name: Woolly Rhinoceros
species.rationale: A low, sturdy body with a two-horn profile and shaggy coat gives Snow an open-ground counterpart to the mammoth.
species.note: Selected still approved. This is a cold-adapted mammal, like the existing mammoth; it needs exposed forage. No production bank or qualification is claimed.

habitat.evidence: Genomic research identifies a cold-adapted megaherbivore and candidate adaptations to low temperatures. Museum evidence links its teeth and coat to tough steppe forage and cold conditions.
habitat.caveat: This is a mammal, not a dinosaur, as is the existing mammoth. It needs open forage rather than only woodland, deep snow or ice.
habitat.recommendation: Add alongside the mammoth in an open, windswept grass-and-sedge clearing with patchy snow.

sources.title: Lord et al. 2020 — Woolly rhinoceros cold adaptation and genomic history
Cardiff University — Author repository and abstract for Lord et al. 2020
Reading Museum — Woolly rhinoceros steppe diet and cold adaptation

islands.habitatBrief: Two placements need reconsideration; five remain conditional or uncertain. All residents need accessible vegetation, not a barren glacier.

islands.name: Fernlands
islands.subtitle: Fern meadows, tall browse and Iguanodon’s greener home.

species.name: Rex
species.rationale: A beloved classic and Fernlands’ obvious predator.
species.note: Approved selected look is integrated through ranch and dedicated reveal assets. Final motion, voice, habitat and native acceptance remain separate.

habitat.evidence: Fossil-distribution research supports use of both river-associated and floodplain environments, compatible with a watered clearing-and-woodland mosaic.
habitat.caveat: Compatibility is an inference; it does not establish a fern-meadow specialization or historical coexistence with every island resident.
habitat.recommendation: Keep; include open ground, wooded edges and freshwater.

sources.title: Lyson & Longrich (2011): Spatial niche partitioning in latest Cretaceous dinosaurs

species.name: Trike
species.rationale: Frill and three horns make a familiar friendly anchor.
species.note: Approved selected look is integrated through ranch and dedicated reveal assets. Final motion, voice, habitat and native acceptance remain separate.

habitat.evidence: Ceratopsian remains preferentially occur in floodplain deposits; the study interprets Triceratops and relatives as using areas farther from river channels.
habitat.caveat: This is a fossil-distribution habitat inference, not proof of an exclusive preference for ferns or treeless meadow.
habitat.recommendation: Keep on firm, vegetated clearings with woodland nearby.

sources.title: Lyson & Longrich (2011): Spatial niche partitioning in latest Cretaceous dinosaurs

species.name: Ankylosaurus
species.rationale: Keeps Anky in the game and fills a low armored role.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Latest working Fernlands assignment replaces Heterodontosaurus; use original green identity.

habitat.evidence: Known from latest Cretaceous terrestrial assemblages; detailed review notes sparse fossils and unresolved preference between preserved coastal plains and less-preserved habitats.
habitat.caveat: Its occurrence in a formation does not establish floodplain or fern-meadow specialization; an upland preference remains a hypothesis.
habitat.recommendation: Keep provisionally with firm ground and varied low vegetation; label habitat preference uncertain.

sources.title: Arbour & Mallon (2017): Anatomy and palaeoecology of Ankylosaurus magniventris

species.name: Stegosaurus
species.rationale: The big coral plates complete a recognisable classics island.
species.note: New animation package required; compare broad plates with Forest Kentrosaurus and Stegouros.

habitat.evidence: Museum research supports feeding on ferns and cycads; its Morrison environments included fern groundcover, conifers and strongly seasonal river landscapes.
habitat.caveat: The widespread Morrison Formation contained varied environments; avoid depicting every resident as a permanent humid-jungle animal.
habitat.recommendation: Keep; fern-rich clearings with occasional conifers are a particularly good match.

sources.title: Natural History Museum: Dinosaur eating-habit insights from Stegosaurus stenops
Natural History Museum: Stegosaurus lifestyle and environment

species.name: Iguanodon
species.rationale: Keeps your Iguanodon in fern-rich, wooded meadows with freshwater, replacing Concavenator’s draft slot.
species.note: Dedicated reveal is integrated locally and passed source checks/visual review. Approved-design ranch actions and complete source-package integration remain pending. Final Frozair visual, full hatch UI and Android/iPhone acceptance are separate. Approved website still and Fernlands home stay unchanged.

habitat.evidence: Iguanodon bernissartensis habitat research documents varied western European plant communities, including fern- and conifer-rich lake margins and seasonal wetland settings. Fernlands’ stated mosaic supplies a supported greener setting.
habitat.caveat: This supports fit to a varied vegetated landscape, not an exclusive fern-meadow preference. The animal’s documented habitat flexibility does not establish its full climatic tolerance.
habitat.recommendation: Keep in Fernlands with ferns, tall tree groves, freshwater margins and firm ground.

sources.title: Rodriguez-Barreiro et al. 2024 — Iguanodon habitat and diet reconstruction

species.name: Brachio
species.rationale: Your requested Fernlands long-neck. Proposed to take Iguanodon’s place, keeping the classic Stegosaurus.
species.note: Older committed ranch/reveal package exists; its approved selected design still needs an asset redo. Selected softer-smile concept. Existing Brachio bank remains a separate production asset.

habitat.evidence: Natural History Museum identifies Brachiosaurus as a high browser thought to feed on tall conifers and tree ferns.
habitat.caveat: Fern groundcover alone is insufficient; tall-tree browsing is an inference from anatomy, not a preserved complete menu.
habitat.recommendation: Keep the requested move; provide substantial tall trees around the fern clearings.

sources.title: Natural History Museum: Brachiosaurus

species.name: Microraptor
species.rationale: Four feather panels make a striking small collectible.
species.note: Grounded scope only. Hindwing and fan-tail clearance need work; no flight mechanic selected.

habitat.evidence: Microraptor comes from Jehol forest environments; aerodynamic models support gliding capability, making woodland structure a sound design choice.
habitat.caveat: A treeless fern field would omit the woodland structure supported by its fossils and functional studies.
habitat.recommendation: Keep only with connected woodland patches and perches; Forest is an alternative if Fernlands stays mostly treeless.

species.name: Anzu
species.rationale: Adds a tall crest and feather-fan silhouette.
species.note: Use selected ivory/chestnut r2, not pink/teal r1. Long arms and fan clearance remain open.

habitat.evidence: Its original description proposes well-watered floodplain preference from body-fossil and possible trace-fossil depositional settings, supporting watered Fernlands clearings.
habitat.caveat: The authors explicitly frame this as a hypothesis; exact diet and habitat specialization remain uncertain.
habitat.recommendation: Keep; include shallow freshwater margins and vegetated floodplain clearings.

sources.title: Lamanna et al. (2014): Original description and palaeoecology of Anzu wyliei

islands.habitatBrief: Fern clearings with wooded edges and freshwater. Brachio needs tall browse; Microraptor needs connected trees and perches.

revisionNote: Approved launch roster: eight residents on each of Forest, Giants, Swamp, Snow and Fernlands. Iguanodon belongs in greener Fernlands. The four benched candidates stay outside the 40; their artwork and history are retained.

habitatReview.title: A habitat-led revision.
habitatReview.note: All 40 recommended residents have an individual sourced assessment. The new Snow candidates replace weaker placements, and Iguanodon moves to greener Fernlands. Ratings describe fit to the stated habitat; they are not proven survival limits or production readiness. These animals span different eras and regions, rather than one historical ecosystem.

definitions.detail: Seasonal woodland with open clearings, firm ground and freshwater margins.
A size collection in a varied valley with wooded and open ground plus substantial rivers. Size and ecology are assessed separately.
Warm freshwater wetlands with connected vegetated banks and actual water access. A wetland resident is not automatically a swimmer.
Seasonally snowy woodland and stream edges beside open forage ground. Include shelter, accessible plants and patchy or shallow snow; this cast does not support barren permanent ice.
Fern-rich meadows and clearings with tall tree groves, wooded margins and freshwater. A completely treeless field changes several ratings.

benchedSpecies.name: Borealopelta
benchedSpecies.rationale: Low armor and shoulder spikes give a third clear silhouette.
benchedSpecies.note: Keep the low body and shoulders readable against the snowy ground.

habitat.evidence: Borealopelta markmitchelli's stomach contents directly document fern feeding, with charcoal supporting use of recently disturbed forest vegetation before marine burial.
habitat.caveat: Diet alone cannot establish climate tolerance; one meal does not establish its habitat range or demonstrate snow specialization.
habitat.recommendation: A greener Forest or Fernlands home is better supported; investigate climate evidence before confirming Snow.

sources.title: Brown et al. 2020 — Original research on Borealopelta's stomach contents

benchedSpecies.benchReason: A fern-feeding animal with no established Snow specialization; retain its concept for a greener future slot.

benchedSpecies.name: Cryolophosaurus
benchedSpecies.rationale: Distinctive crest and familiar biped movement, but Antarctic discovery alone does not support Snow; habitat review is open.
benchedSpecies.note: Its head/crest needs to stay distinct from the other pastel bipeds.

habitat.evidence: Cryolophosaurus ellioti's Antarctic locality records an ancient river in warm-temperate forest at high latitude during the Early Jurassic.
habitat.caveat: Ancient Antarctic provenance supports strong light seasonality, not the modern continent's ice climate or demonstrated snow specialization.
habitat.recommendation: Review for Forest or wooded Fernlands; do not use Antarctic discovery alone to justify Snow.

sources.title: Ohio State University Orton Museum — Cryolophosaurus and its ancient environment

benchedSpecies.benchReason: Its ancient Antarctic locality was warm-temperate forest; Antarctic provenance alone does not justify Snow.

benchedSpecies.name: Citipati
benchedSpecies.rationale: A deep beak, crest and paired hands add a playful silhouette.
benchedSpecies.note: Shares an upright pastel role with Cryo and a feathered role with Fernlands Anzu.

habitat.evidence: Citipati osmolskae is known from Ukhaa Tolgod; geological research reconstructs an arid dune environment with ephemeral ponds and lakes.
habitat.caveat: Feathers do not establish cold specialization, and present-day Mongolia's winter climate cannot be transferred directly to its Cretaceous environment.
habitat.recommendation: Review for a drier, vegetated habitat; Snow is a weak evidence-based placement.

sources.title: American Museum of Natural History — Citipati and Ukhaa Tolgod locality
Dingus et al. 2008 — Original geological study of Ukhaa Tolgod

benchedSpecies.benchReason: Its documented locality was an arid dune environment, making Snow a weak evidence-based choice.

benchedSpecies.name: Concavenator
benchedSpecies.rationale: A low hip hump and strong stripes give Fernlands another distinctive predator.
benchedSpecies.note: Selected final comparison; another carnivore beside Rex, not the rejected spotted baby-Rex.

habitat.evidence: Concavenator comes from Las Hoyas, reconstructed by its research team as a Cretaceous wetland ecosystem with aquatic and terrestrial organisms.
habitat.caveat: The carcass underwent some transport; wetland deposition does not establish an aquatic lifestyle or exclusive habitat preference.
habitat.recommendation: Keep near watered, vegetated margins; avoid an entirely dry, exposed meadow interpretation.

sources.title: Universidad Autónoma de Madrid: Las Hoyas, a Cretaceous wetland
Cuesta Fidalgo (2016): Concavenator taphonomic, phylogenetic and morphofunctional analyses

benchedSpecies.benchReason: Benched to give the user’s retained Iguanodon a greener home while preserving eight Fernlands residents. This is a casting-space choice, not a newly discovered habitat mismatch.
